title: The First 100 Days — Head Boy/Girl
theme: School leadership, governance, and navigating power with empathy
description: You've just been elected Head Boy/Girl of your school. Over 10 critical decisions — from handling bullies to allocating budgets — you'll discover what kind of leader you really are. Every choice shapes your legacy.
learning_objectives: Understand how leaders balance competing interests and limited resources
Practice making decisions under pressure with imperfect information
Explore the difference between popularity and effective leadership
how_to_play: Read each scenario carefully and choose the response that feels most natural to you. There are no wrong answers — each choice reveals a different leadership style and has real consequences for your school.

glossary_terms.definition: The process of deciding how to divide limited money across different needs
Any person affected by a decision — students, teachers, parents, staff
Finding a peaceful solution when two people or groups disagree
Taking responsibility for your decisions and their outcomes
What people remember about you after you leave a role or position

rounds.title: Your First Assembly Speech
rounds.situation:
The microphone squeaks as {player_name} adjusts it, and the sound bounces off the concrete walls of the assembly ground. Twelve hundred pairs of eyes stare back — the juniors cross-legged on the dusty ground squinting up at the stage, the seniors leaning against the back wall with folded arms and skeptical half-smiles, teachers lining the sides like referees at a boxing match.

Your hands are trembling slightly. You can feel the laminated Head Boy/Girl badge pinned to your chest — it's heavier than you thought it would be. In the third row, Arjun from Class 10 is mimicking your posture to his friends, getting muffled laughs. Priya, your vice head girl, stands just offstage, giving you an encouraging nod that somehow makes you more nervous.

Behind you on the plastic chair sits Ms. Sharma, the principal, her reading glasses perched on her nose, a pen tapping her knee. She'd pulled you aside ten minutes ago: 'Keep it tight. Talk about discipline and the new attendance policy.' But Ravi, your best friend on the student council, had whispered in the corridor: 'If you open with rules, they'll tune out in ten seconds.'

The last head boy, Rohit, was adored by students — he'd cracked jokes and promised pizza parties — but the teachers thought he was a clown. The one before him was a principal's pet who read government circulars at assembly. Nobody listened to a word. Somewhere between entertainer and bureaucrat lies the leader this school actually needs.

Your speech is scribbled on an index card in your blazer pocket. But there's also a completely different version forming in your head — one that might actually make 1,200 kids care. Three minutes. No do-overs. The mic hums, waiting.
rounds.story: Your predecessor Rohit was popular but left behind nothing — no systems, no changes, just a trail of broken promises about vending machines and shorter assemblies. The teachers are wary. The students are bored. And Ms. Sharma has made it quietly clear that she expects this year to be different. This is the moment where the school decides who you are.
rounds.image_prompt: Indian student standing at podium in school assembly, microphone in hand, large crowd of students in uniforms watching expectantly
rounds.coaching_moment: The first impression a leader makes sets the tone for everything that follows — choose what you stand for, not just what people want to hear.

choices.label: Promise exciting events and changes
choices.description: Pocket the index card. Lean into the mic and announce a school carnival next month, relaxed uniform Saturdays, and a complete canteen overhaul. Paint a picture of the best year this school has ever had. Watch the energy ripple through the crowd like a wave.
choices.consequence_hint: Students will love it, but teachers may see you as unserious and the principal may be disappointed

events.description: The assembly ground erupts. Students stamp their feet and cheer. Ravi pumps his fist from the side. But you catch Ms. Sharma exchanging a long, slow look with Mr. Gupta, the sports teacher — the kind of look that says 'here we go again.' Priya whispers as you step off stage: 'That was electric. But you just made about twenty promises. How many can we actually keep?'

choices.label: Talk about responsibility and standards
choices.description: Pull out the index card. Speak clearly about what this school can become — cleaner corridors, better attendance, academic targets, a culture of accountability. Set expectations with a steady voice. Look the seniors in the eye when you say 'this starts with us.'
choices.consequence_hint: Teachers and principal will respect you, but students may find you boring and preachy

events.description: Ms. Sharma nods slowly, a rare flicker of approval crossing her face. Mr. Gupta straightens up from his slouch against the pillar. But in the back rows, a low murmur spreads. Arjun from Class 10 stage-whispers loud enough for half the ground to hear: 'Great, another principal's pet.' A few students laugh. Priya catches your eye from offstage, her expression unreadable.

choices.label: Share a personal story and ask for ideas
choices.description: Forget both scripts. Tell them about that time in Class 8 when you were new, lonely, eating lunch alone behind the library — until a senior you barely knew sat down next to you. Tell them that's the school you want to build. Then ask every class to submit one suggestion by Friday. One idea per class. No idea too small.
choices.consequence_hint: This builds connection and trust, but managing 40+ class suggestions will be a lot of work

events.description: Something shifts in the assembly ground. The juniors stop fidgeting. A Class 6 girl in the front row is looking up at you like you're speaking directly to her. Several teachers smile — even Mr. Gupta uncrosses his arms. By Wednesday, the suggestion box outside the staff room is overflowing. Priya spends her lunch hour sorting through them, shaking her head in amazement: 'There's forty-three. We actually have to read all of these.'

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: The Bully Complaint
rounds.situation:
It's the Thursday after your assembly speech, and {player_name} is eating lunch in the student council room when the door creaks open. A small girl — she can't be more than twelve — stands in the doorway, her eyes red and swollen, her lower lip trembling. Her name tag reads 'Riya — VII-B.'

She doesn't sit down. She stands there, clutching her empty tiffin bag like a shield, and the story comes out in fragments between hiccups. Three boys from Class 9 have been taking her tiffin box every day for two weeks. They hide it — sometimes in the dustbin, sometimes on the roof of the bathroom block. They call her 'Riya Roti' because she brings rotis from home while they buy burgers from the canteen. Yesterday, they told her if she reported them, they'd make sure her younger brother in Class 5 'has the same experience.'

The worst part: one of the three boys is Kunal Mehta. School basketball captain. Star of the inter-school tournament. The boy whose photo is on the trophy cabinet in the front lobby. Mr. Gupta, the sports teacher, treats him like a son.

Riya looks up at {player_name} with an expression that is equal parts hope and terror. 'Please don't tell anyone my name,' she whispers. 'They'll know it was me.' Her hands are shaking. Outside the window, you can see Kunal and his friends laughing by the water cooler, shoving each other playfully, completely unaware that their world might be about to shift.
rounds.story: This is the first real test of your leadership. The assembly speech was performance — this is the substance underneath. Every prefect, every student council member, every teacher is going to learn about how you handled this, and it will define what they think you stand for. Ravi told you at lunch yesterday: 'The last head boy never dealt with a single bullying case. He just forwarded everything to the discipline teacher and forgot about it.'
rounds.image_prompt: Younger Indian student crying while talking to an older student leader in a school corridor, other students in background
rounds.coaching_moment: True leadership is tested not when you have to choose between right and wrong, but when doing the right thing has a personal cost.

choices.label: Take it directly to the principal
choices.description: Walk straight to Ms. Sharma's office, Riya's account written out in detail. Names, dates, specifics. The formal route — let the institution handle it with its full authority. Tell Riya you'll protect her, even as you hand over control of the situation.
choices.consequence_hint: The bullies will face consequences, but Riya may feel exposed and the sports captain's friends may resent you

events.description: Ms. Sharma's face hardens as she reads your note. She calls the three boys in within the hour. Kunal walks out of her office looking pale, his jaw tight. But by afternoon, Riya is sitting alone in the classroom, hugging her knees — someone told the boys it was her. She won't look at you in the corridor. Mr. Gupta corners you near the staff room: 'You could have talked to me first. Kunal's a good kid who made a mistake. Now his tournament eligibility is under review.'

choices.label: Talk to the boys privately first
choices.description: Find Kunal and the other two during the games period. Pull them behind the basketball court, away from their friends. No teachers, no formal complaints. Look Kunal in the eye and tell him exactly what he's doing to a twelve-year-old girl. Describe the fear. Describe the shaking hands. Give them one chance to stop — and make clear what happens if they don't.
choices.consequence_hint: This gives them a chance to change but risks them not taking you seriously or continuing when you're not watching

events.description: Kunal's smirk fades about thirty seconds into the conversation. He wasn't expecting this — not the confrontation, but the specifics. The trembling hands. The threat against her brother. His friend Sahil stares at the ground. 'We were just messing around,' Kunal says, but his voice has lost its swagger. You tell him messing around doesn't make a seventh-grader cry every morning before school. There's a long silence. Kunal nods once, sharply, and walks away. Priya, who watched from a distance, says quietly: 'That took guts. But what if they don't stop?'

choices.label: Set up an anonymous reporting system
choices.description: Don't name Riya. Instead, use this as the spark for something bigger. Draft a proposal for an anonymous complaint box — painted bright yellow, mounted outside the library where everyone passes. Announce it at the next assembly as a school-wide anti-bullying initiative. Protect Riya by making her one voice among many.
choices.consequence_hint: This protects Riya's identity and builds a lasting system, but won't solve her immediate problem today

events.description: The bright yellow complaint box goes up outside the library by Thursday, with a sign that reads 'Your Voice Matters — Anonymous & Safe.' Riya walks past it every day, and on the second day, she slips a folded note inside with a tiny smile. By the end of the first week, three other students have submitted reports — a Class 6 boy being extorted for lunch money, a Class 8 girl whose lab partner keeps 'accidentally' breaking her things, and a note that simply says 'thank you for listening.' But Kunal is still taking Riya's tiffin. The system is building, but Riya is still hungry at lunch.

expert_pick.reason: Leadership experts recommend thinking several moves ahead before committing.

rounds.title: Teacher-Student Conflict
rounds.situation:
It's been ten days since the bully complaint, and {player_name} is still thinking about it when a new crisis lands. The student council room door bangs open during lunch, and seven Class 11 students pour in, led by Neha Kapoor — the class topper who never raises her voice. Today, she's practically shaking with anger.

'Mrs. Deshpande gave our entire class zero on the chemistry assignment,' Neha says, her voice cracking. 'The entire class. Because Rohit, Sameer, and Dev copied from the internet.' She pulls out her assignment — {player_name} can see the hand-drawn molecular diagrams, the color-coded reactions, the bibliography at the back. Two weeks of work. Zero marks.

Mrs. Deshpande is a legend at this school. Twenty-two years of teaching. She once made the principal's son redo an exam because she suspected him of looking at his neighbor's paper. The teachers' room calls her 'The Iron Lady' behind her back, half in admiration, half in fear. She's never reversed a grade in her career.

But this feels different. Neha's eyes are filling with tears. Behind her, Akash — a quiet boy who barely speaks in class — mumbles, 'I spent my entire Diwali break on that assignment.' Priya, who's been listening from the corner, catches your eye with a look that says: this one's going to be messy no matter what you do.

The staff room is thirty steps away. Mrs. Deshpande is probably in there right now, sipping her afternoon chai, fully aware that the storm is coming.
rounds.story: After the way you handled the bullying situation, students are starting to see you as someone who actually does something. That's both a gift and a burden — because now they're bringing you problems that put you directly between a teacher's authority and a student's legitimate pain. Ravi warned you: 'Once they start coming to you, they won't stop.'
rounds.image_prompt: Group of upset Indian students talking to student leader outside classroom, chemistry lab visible in background
rounds.coaching_moment: Navigating between authority figures and peers without alienating either side is one of the hardest leadership skills to master.

choices.label: Request a meeting with Mrs. Deshpande
choices.description: Walk to the staff room alone. Knock on the door. Ask Mrs. Deshpande if she has five minutes. Sit across from her with your hands folded and your voice respectful, and lay out what the honest students are feeling. Don't challenge her authority — just present what you've seen. Neha's diagrams. Akash's Diwali break. Ask if there's a way to separate the innocent from the guilty.
choices.consequence_hint: Mrs. Deshpande might appreciate the maturity, or she might see it as students undermining her authority

events.description: Mrs. Deshpande listens without interrupting, her chai going cold in her hands. When you finish, she's quiet for a long moment. 'I've been teaching for twenty-two years,' she says. 'No student has ever come to talk to me like this — with evidence, not just complaints.' She doesn't promise anything. But she takes Neha's assignment from your hands and looks at it properly for the first time. 'Let me think about it,' she says. The students wait outside the council room all afternoon, anxious, checking their phones every two minutes.

choices.label: Tell students to accept the punishment
choices.description: Close the council room door. Look Neha in the eye and tell her the truth as you see it: Mrs. Deshpande has her reasons. Collective punishment stings, but it also teaches the class to hold each other accountable. Tell them that challenging a teacher publicly will only make things worse — and that learning to absorb unfairness with dignity is itself a lesson.
choices.consequence_hint: Teachers will see you as mature, but students will feel abandoned by their own leader

events.description: The room goes cold. Neha stares at you for three full seconds, then picks up her zero-marked assignment from the table. 'I thought you were different,' she says quietly, and walks out. Akash follows without a word. In the corridor, you hear someone mutter loud enough for you to catch: 'What's the point of having a Head Boy/Girl who won't stand up for us?' Priya stays behind, arms crossed: 'You might be right. But you just lost seven people who believed in you.'

choices.label: Escalate to the principal with both sides
choices.description: Spend the evening writing a careful, one-page note to Ms. Sharma. On the left: Mrs. Deshpande's reasoning and her right to enforce academic integrity. On the right: the impact on students who did original work, with specific examples. Request a three-way meeting — teacher, students, and principal — to find a fair resolution. Sign it formally as Head Boy/Girl.
choices.consequence_hint: This is thorough but going over a teacher's head can damage your relationship with the staff

events.description: Ms. Sharma reads your note the next morning and schedules a meeting for Friday. Word travels fast in the staff room — by lunch, Mrs. Deshpande knows you went over her head. She doesn't say anything to you directly, but when you pass her in the corridor, her greeting is noticeably cooler. Mr. Gupta pulls you aside: 'Be careful. The staff room has a long memory.' Priya looks worried: 'You did the right thing on paper. But Mrs. Deshpande will remember this for the rest of the year.'

expert_pick.reason: Leadership experts recommend thinking several moves ahead before committing.

rounds.title: The Discipline Dilemma
rounds.situation:
The corridor outside the Class 10 rooms smells like floor cleaner and trouble. {player_name} arrives to find a circle of students parting like a wave, and in the center: Vikram with a split lip and clenched fists, Arun with a bloody nose and a torn collar, and a terrified Class 6 kid pressed against the wall who saw the whole thing.

The story comes together in pieces over the next hour. Vikram threw the first punch — there's no dispute about that. He caught Arun outside the boys' bathroom and hit him hard enough to slam his head against the wall. But the reason is what makes this complicated. For three weeks, Arun has been telling anyone who'll listen that Vikram's father lost his job, that his family had to sell their car, that they might lose their house. None of this is confirmed. Some of it might be true. All of it has made Vikram's life miserable — the whispers when he walks into class, the pointed jokes about 'people who can't afford things.'

Vikram sits in the discipline room staring at the floor, jaw clenched so hard you can see the muscles twitching. He hasn't cried, but he's close. Arun is in the medical room getting his nose checked, loudly telling anyone who'll listen that Vikram is 'psycho' and 'should be expelled.'

The discipline committee — three teachers including Mr. Gupta — has gathered in the staff room. They want {player_name}'s recommendation before they send theirs to Ms. Sharma. Whatever you suggest, the principal will almost certainly approve. Priya is waiting outside the door: 'Both of them are wrong. But are they equally wrong? That's the question everyone's going to judge you on.'
rounds.story: After the chemistry assignment situation and the bullying case, the school is watching closely. You've built a reputation — now it's being tested. Ravi texted you: 'Everyone's talking about this. Whatever you decide, own it.' This isn't just about two boys anymore. It's about what kind of justice system this school has.
rounds.image_prompt: Two Indian school boys being separated after a fight, student leader looking on thoughtfully, other students watching
rounds.coaching_moment: Justice isn't always about punishing equally — sometimes it's about understanding unequally and responding proportionally.

choices.label: Equal punishment for both
choices.description: Stand in front of the discipline committee and say it plainly: three-day suspension for both. Violence is violence — Vikram's fist crossed a line. And rumor-spreading is harassment — Arun's words crossed a different line. Equal offense, equal consequence. No exceptions, no special treatment, no grey areas.
choices.consequence_hint: This is fair on paper but Vikram's supporters will say you ignored months of provocation

events.description: Both boys are suspended for three days. The announcement goes up on the notice board by 4 PM. Vikram walks out of school with his bag slung over one shoulder, not looking at anyone. His mother calls the school within the hour, her voice tight with anger: 'My son was being tormented for weeks and you punished him the same as the boy who did it?' Arun's friends high-five in the corridor — to them, equal punishment means Arun got away light. Priya catches you after school: 'The decision is defensible. But defensible isn't the same as right.'

choices.label: Different consequences for each
choices.description: Lay it out for the committee in detail: Vikram gets a formal warning for violence — no suspension, because three weeks of targeted harassment is a mitigating factor. Arun gets a formal warning for bullying plus four mandatory sessions with the school counselor. Both boys must write a letter of apology — Vikram for his fists, Arun for his words. Both letters get read aloud to each other, not the school.
choices.consequence_hint: This acknowledges the full picture but some will call it inconsistent or soft

events.description: The school counselor, Mrs. Rao, meets both boys separately that week. She tells you later, quietly: 'Arun broke down in the second session. He didn't realize what his words were doing — he thought it was just gossip.' Vikram's apology letter is three lines long and stiff, but Arun's is two pages. Mr. Gupta grumbles in the staff room that 'a punch should mean suspension, full stop,' but most teachers nod when they hear the reasoning. Arun looks genuinely surprised that anyone took the rumor-spreading seriously enough to call it bullying.

choices.label: Restorative justice — mediated conversation
choices.description: Skip the formal punishment track entirely. Propose something the school has never tried: a restorative justice circle. Bring Vikram and Arun into the counselor's room with Mrs. Rao as mediator. Let Vikram explain what those three weeks felt like. Let Arun hear it without being able to deflect. No suspension, no black marks — just two boys facing each other's pain and agreeing on a way forward.
choices.consequence_hint: This is progressive and healing, but some teachers will say you're being too soft on a fistfight

events.description: The mediation session is brutal for the first twenty minutes. Vikram won't look at Arun. Arun keeps saying 'I was just joking' until Mrs. Rao asks him to repeat what he said about Vikram's family, slowly, word by word. Arun can't finish the sentence. Something cracks open in the room. Vikram finally speaks: 'My dad cries at night. You made it a joke in the canteen.' The session ends with a handshake — not warm, but real. Outside, Mr. Gupta shakes his head: 'Give it a week. They'll be at each other's throats again.' Priya says nothing, but she's smiling.

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: The Fallout — Strict Approach
rounds.situation:
It's been one week since the suspensions, and the fallout has settled into something {player_name} didn't expect. The nickname arrived first — whispered in corridors, scrawled on the back of a bathroom stall, and finally said to your face by a Class 10 kid who didn't realize you were standing behind him: 'The Enforcer.'

Three prefects — Manish, Tara, and Deepa — leave their resignation letters on your desk on Monday morning. Tara's is the longest: 'I became a prefect to help students, not to be part of a system that punishes people without listening to their side. I'm sorry, but I can't represent this council anymore.' By lunch, a WhatsApp group called 'Students Against the Council' has 200 members.

But here's what's strange: the staff room is a different world. Mrs. Deshpande, who hasn't spoken to you warmly since the chemistry assignment incident, stops you in the corridor and says, 'That discipline decision took courage.' Mr. Gupta claps you on the shoulder in the parking lot. Even Ms. Sharma calls you in and says she wants you to draft a student code of conduct for next term — 'something with teeth,' she says, sliding a blank document across her desk.

Priya finds you staring at the resignations after school. 'You have the teachers,' she says carefully. 'But you're losing the students. You can't lead a school where half the population thinks you're their warden.' The blank document sits on the desk. The principal needs a draft by end of week.
rounds.story: Your strict stance has created two realities. In the staff room, you're respected. In the corridors, you're feared. The question isn't whether you were right — it's whether being right is enough when the people you're supposed to represent feel unheard. Ravi hasn't said much all week, which is unusual. When you ask him, he just says: 'I think you need to decide if you're the students' leader or the school's enforcer. They're not the same thing.'
rounds.image_prompt: Indian student leader at a desk drafting a document, some students looking unhappy in background, teachers looking supportive
rounds.coaching_moment: Firmness without explanation becomes authoritarianism. Firmness with transparency becomes respected governance.
rounds.timer_narrative: The principal needs your draft by end of day...

choices.label: Draft a strict, clear code of conduct
choices.description: Sit down and write it properly — clean rules, defined consequences, escalation tiers. Zero tolerance for violence, bullying, and academic dishonesty. Every offense has a prescribed response. No ambiguity, no room for interpretation. This school needs structure, and you're going to give it structure. Deliver it to Ms. Sharma by Thursday.
choices.consequence_hint: Teachers love it, students feel unheard — the gap between you and your peers grows wider

events.description: Ms. Sharma approves the code the same day, barely changing a comma. It goes up on the notice board Friday morning in laminated sheets. By Friday evening, the 'Students Against the Council' WhatsApp group has 400 members and a new name: 'Students Against the Code.' Someone pins a photocopy of the code to the canteen bulletin board with red marker circles around the harshest clauses and a note: 'Written by someone who forgot they're a student too.' Ravi takes it down before you see it, but Priya tells you. She doesn't sugarcoat it: 'You wrote a perfect document. But nobody asked the people it applies to.'

choices.label: Add student input to the process
choices.description: Go back to Ms. Sharma and ask for one more week. Tell her you'll draft the code, but first you want to hold a class-representative meeting — every class sends one voice. Let the students help shape the rules that will govern them. It'll be messy and slow, but a code that students helped write is a code they might actually follow.
choices.consequence_hint: This slows the process but could produce a code that students actually respect

events.description: The class-rep meeting happens in the school auditorium on Wednesday afternoon, and it's chaos for the first twenty minutes. Everyone talks at once. A Class 9 rep says the code should ban homework on weekends. A Class 12 rep says juniors should lose phone privileges. Arjun from Class 10 stands up and says, 'Why should we follow rules we didn't vote for?' — and for once, he has a point. Priya moderates, and slowly, something remarkable happens: the students start editing each other's ideas, finding compromises, building something together. By the end, you have a draft that's tougher than expected — because the students chose the standards themselves. Tara, one of the prefects who resigned, asks to rejoin the council.

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: The Fallout — Compassionate Approach
rounds.situation:
A week after the mediation, {player_name} is shelving files in the student council room when two sharp knocks sound on the door. It's Mr. Gupta, the sports teacher, filling the doorframe with his broad shoulders, and behind him, Mrs. Deshpande — a combination that usually means trouble for someone.

Mr. Gupta doesn't sit. He stands with his arms crossed and gets straight to the point: 'I've been teaching here for fifteen years. I've seen what happens when students think they can throw punches and walk away with a chat and a handshake. Discipline collapses. I've already had two Class 9 boys shoving each other in the corridor yesterday saying, "What's the worst that happens — a talking-to?"'

Mrs. Deshpande is quieter but sharper: 'I respect what you were trying to do. But you set a precedent. Every student in this school now knows that a fistfight gets you a conversation, not a consequence. What message does that send?'

The sports coach adds, leaning forward: 'Vikram needs to understand that violence has a price. Not just a heart-to-heart. A real price. Otherwise the next kid who gets angry will think punching is an option.'

They're both looking at {player_name} expectantly. Through the window, you can see Vikram and Arun walking in different directions across the courtyard — not friends, but not enemies either. The mediation worked. But the teachers don't see that. They see a precedent they're afraid of.
rounds.story: Word of your compassionate approach has spread in two very different ways. Among students, you're becoming known as someone who listens — someone who sees people, not just rule-breakers. But in the staff room, a different narrative is forming: that the new Head Boy/Girl is soft, that discipline is eroding, that the mediation was a nice idea that won't survive contact with reality. Priya told you this morning: 'You did something good. Now you have to defend it.'
rounds.image_prompt: Indian student leader facing two stern teachers in a staff room, looking composed but under pressure
rounds.coaching_moment: Compassion in leadership is only sustainable when paired with clear boundaries — otherwise it becomes avoidance.
rounds.timer_narrative: The teachers expect a response before the next staff meeting...

choices.label: Stand by your decision firmly
choices.description: Look them both in the eye. Take a breath. Then explain, calmly and without apologizing, that the mediation produced a result that three days of suspension never would have — Arun understood the damage of his words, Vikram was heard, and neither boy left the room feeling like the system failed them. Tell them you believe in consequences, but you also believe in the right consequences for the right situation. Don't flinch.
choices.consequence_hint: Students will trust you more, but some teachers may work around you on future discipline issues

events.description: The room is silent for a long moment. Mr. Gupta's jaw tightens. Mrs. Deshpande studies you over her reading glasses — the same look she gives students she's re-evaluating. Finally, Mr. Gupta exhales through his nose: 'Alright. Let's see how it plays out. But if there's another fight next month, I'm going straight to the principal.' They leave. Priya, who was listening from the corridor, slips in: 'That was the hardest room you've walked into so far. And you didn't blink.' Ravi texts you that night: 'Heard you stood your ground with Gupta. Respect.'

choices.label: Add follow-up consequences
choices.description: Acknowledge their concern — genuinely, not performatively. Then propose a middle path: keep the mediation as the foundation, but add a one-week probation for both boys with mandatory check-ins every two days. If either boy causes any issue during probation, the full disciplinary process kicks in automatically. Show them you're compassionate but not naive — that you can hold two ideas at once.
choices.consequence_hint: This satisfies teachers without betraying your original approach — a pragmatic middle ground

events.description: Mr. Gupta's shoulders drop half an inch — the teacher equivalent of a standing ovation. Mrs. Deshpande nods: 'That's reasonable. Structure around compassion.' The probation framework gets posted on the discipline board. Vikram checks in dutifully, almost relieved to have a clear path. Arun is more resistant but complies after Mrs. Rao explains the alternative. By the end of the week, even Mr. Gupta admits grudgingly to Priya: 'The probation thing was smart. I still think the kid should've been suspended, but at least there's a system.' It's not total victory. But it's something rarer — a compromise that nobody hates.

expert_pick.reason: The most effective leaders adapt their approach based on the situation — not habit.

rounds.title: Annual Day — Budget Crisis
rounds.situation:
The Annual Day planning committee meets in the school auditorium on a Tuesday afternoon, and within fifteen minutes, {player_name} realizes this is going to be the most politically charged meeting of the term. Three teachers sit across the table, each with a folder, each absolutely certain that their department's needs are the most important thing in the building.

Mrs. Fernandes, the drama teacher — a small woman with enormous energy who directed last year's play that still gets talked about — slides her budget across: ₹80,000. Full-scale production of a Hindi adaptation of Twelve Angry Men. Costumes, set design, professional lighting. 'This is the one event parents actually attend,' she says, tapping the table. 'This is how the school is judged.'

Mr. Gupta is next. He doesn't slide — he drops his folder: ₹60,000. Inter-school basketball and athletics competition fees, travel costs, new jerseys. The deadline for fee payment is in three weeks. 'If we don't pay, we forfeit,' he says flatly. 'Two years of building this team, gone.'

Then Mr. Nair, the music teacher, soft-spoken and perpetually overlooked: ₹40,000. A new sound system. The current one — held together with tape and prayers — crackled through the entire Independence Day program. 'Every event in this school runs through speakers,' he says quietly. 'And ours are dying.'

Total requests: ₹1,80,000. Total budget: ₹1,50,000. {player_name} is staring at a gap of ₹30,000 and three teachers who each believe — with genuine conviction — that their need is non-negotiable. Priya slides you a note under the table: 'There's no right answer here. Just different kinds of disappointment.'
rounds.story: This is the first time you're making a decision that involves real money and real consequences for people's work. The bully complaint tested your ethics. The discipline case tested your judgment. This tests something different: your ability to allocate scarce resources when everyone's need is legitimate. Ravi told you after last night's council meeting: 'Budget fights are where school politics gets ugly. Teachers remember who funded them and who didn't.'
rounds.image_prompt: Indian student leader looking at budget papers with three teachers waiting expectantly, calculator and spreadsheets visible
rounds.coaching_moment: Resource allocation is where leadership gets real — you can't please everyone, so you must decide what matters most.
rounds.timer_narrative: The vendors need confirmed orders by tomorrow...

choices.label: Cut each request proportionally
choices.description: Pull out a calculator in front of all three teachers. Show the math: ₹1,80,000 requested, ₹1,50,000 available. Propose a flat 17% reduction across the board — drama gets ₹66,400, sports gets ₹49,800, music gets ₹33,200. Nobody gets everything. Nobody gets nothing. The math is fair even if the feelings aren't.
choices.consequence_hint: Nobody is fully happy, but nobody is left out — the drama might be simpler and the sound system older

events.description: The room goes quiet as you lay out the spreadsheet. Mrs. Fernandes stares at the numbers, doing mental math on which costumes she can cut. Mr. Gupta's jaw tightens — ₹49,800 means the team travels by state bus instead of private coach. Mr. Nair just nods, as if he expected to be cut and is grateful it wasn't worse. 'I'll make it work,' Mrs. Fernandes says finally, gathering her folder. 'I always do.' It's not enthusiasm. But it's acceptance. Priya exhales as they file out: 'Nobody's happy. But nobody's plotting against you either. For a budget meeting, that's a win.'

choices.label: Prioritize the competition fees
choices.description: Make the hard call. The sports competition has an external deadline — if the fees aren't paid, the school forfeits and two years of Mr. Gupta's coaching goes to waste. Fund sports fully at ₹60,000. Split the remaining ₹90,000 between drama and music. Tell Mrs. Fernandes and Mr. Nair the truth: their work matters, but a deadline is a deadline.
choices.consequence_hint: The sports team is thrilled, but the drama and music teachers feel their work is seen as less important

events.description: Mr. Gupta almost smiles — the closest thing to joy you've seen on his face all year. The basketball team qualifies for state-level two weeks later, and the trophy goes into the cabinet next to Kunal's photo. But the drama production tells a different story: Mrs. Fernandes performs a scaled-down version with borrowed props and costumes stitched from old curtains. It's still good — she's too talented for it not to be — but everyone can see what's missing. Mr. Nair patches the old speakers one more time. During the Annual Day, the right channel cuts out during the chief guest's speech. Priya winces from the front row.

choices.label: Fundraise the gap
choices.description: Stand up from the table and say something none of them expect: 'What if we don't cut anyone?' Propose a school fundraiser — a weekend food festival organized by the student council, with stalls run by each class, a talent show with a ₹50 entry fee, and a parent contribution drive. Raise the extra ₹30,000 yourselves. Fund everything. Sleep less.
choices.consequence_hint: This funds everything but requires significant organizing effort and might not raise enough in time

events.description: The fundraiser takes over your life for two weeks. Priya handles the food stall permits. Ravi sweet-talks the local samosa vendor into donating 200 samosas at cost. Arjun from Class 10 — of all people — turns out to be brilliant at selling raffle tickets, charming parents with a smile you've never seen him use at school. The talent show draws a crowd. A Class 7 kid does a magic trick that goes wrong in the most hilarious way possible, and the laughter alone feels worth the effort. Final count: ₹35,400 raised. All three departments get full funding. Mrs. Fernandes hugs you in the corridor. Mr. Nair sends a handwritten thank-you note. You haven't slept more than five hours a night in two weeks, but something in the school feels different — like people pulled together for the first time.

expert_pick.reason: Leadership experts recommend thinking several moves ahead before committing.

rounds.title: Library vs. Sports Ground
rounds.situation:
The email arrives on a Wednesday morning and changes everything. A 1998 alumnus — now a tech entrepreneur in Bangalore — has donated ₹2,00,000 to the school 'for improvement.' No restrictions, no strings, no pet project. Just a cheque and a note: 'This school made me. I want to give back. Use it where it matters most.'

Ms. Sharma forwards the email to {player_name} with a single line: 'I'd like the student council's recommendation by Friday.'

Friday. Two days to decide how to spend more money than the school has seen in a single donation in years. And immediately, two camps form.

The library is a tragedy. {player_name} walks through it during lunch — broken MDF shelves held together with duct tape, a 'New Arrivals' section whose newest book is from 2016, three tube lights out of six flickering, chairs with stuffing coming out. A Class 8 girl sits in the corner reading a novel with the cover falling off, her bag propped against a shelf to keep it from wobbling. The librarian, Mrs. Patil, has been writing grant requests for four years. All denied.

But the sports ground is dangerous. The basketball court surface is cracked in three places — Kunal twisted his ankle on one of the cracks last month. The football field has potholes that fill with water during monsoon and become invisible. Two students were injured this term. Mr. Gupta has been filing safety complaints since August. The inter-school tournament is eight weeks away, and the visiting teams' coaches have already commented on the state of the ground.

Two genuine needs. One pot of money. Priya drops two folders on your desk — one labeled LIBRARY, one labeled SPORTS GROUND — each with cost estimates, photos, and student testimonials. 'I'm not going to tell you which one to choose,' she says. 'But I'll tell you this: whichever one you don't choose is going to feel betrayed.'
rounds.story: After the Annual Day budget crisis, everyone knows {player_name} is the person who makes the hard calls on money. That reputation cuts both ways — people trust your judgment, but they also hold you personally responsible for the outcome. Ravi said it bluntly at council meeting: 'The budget thing was ₹30,000. This is ₹2,00,000. The stakes just went up by a factor of seven, and so did the number of people who'll be angry at you.'
rounds.image_prompt: Split image showing a run-down library with broken shelves on one side and a damaged sports ground with potholes on the other, Indian school setting
rounds.coaching_moment: When both options are genuinely needed, the best leaders make their reasoning transparent, not just their decision.
rounds.timer_narrative: The donor wants to see a proposal by Friday...

choices.label: Renovate the library
choices.description: Write the proposal with conviction: the library is the intellectual heart of this school. Every student, every subject, every exam — it all runs through books and knowledge. New shelves, 500 new books, a digital catalog system, a reading corner with beanbags and good lighting. Transform a ruin into a sanctuary. The sports ground can wait for the next donation.
choices.consequence_hint: Academic-minded students and teachers celebrate, but athletes feel sidelined again

events.description: The library transformation takes three weeks and it's stunning. New wooden shelves, warm lighting, 500 books with that intoxicating new-paper smell. The Class 8 girl who used to read in the broken corner now has a beanbag by the window. Mrs. Patil cries on the opening day — quietly, turning away so the students don't see. But across the campus, the athletes practice on the same cracked court, the same potholed field. Kunal limps off the basketball court on Thursday with a re-aggravated ankle. Mr. Gupta doesn't say anything to you. He doesn't need to. The silence is louder than any complaint.

choices.label: Fix the sports ground
choices.description: Safety isn't negotiable. Write the proposal around the most urgent argument: students are getting injured. The basketball court needs resurfacing, the football field potholes need filling, and the running track needs new lane markings before the inter-school tournament. Every day the ground stays broken is a day someone could get hurt. The library has survived eight years — it can survive a few more months.
choices.consequence_hint: Athletes are overjoyed, but the library continues to deteriorate and bookish students feel invisible

events.description: The contractors arrive on Monday. By the end of two weeks, the basketball court gleams with fresh paint and smooth concrete. The football field is level for the first time in years. The running track has crisp white lanes. The sports teams practice with a swagger they haven't had all year — Mr. Gupta actually whistles while setting up cones. But a week later, a letter appears in your suggestion box, written in careful cursive on ruled paper: 'Dear Head Boy/Girl, I spend every free period in the library because I don't have friends and books are the only thing that make school bearable. The shelf near the window collapsed yesterday. A Class 8 girl named Meena wrote it. Priya reads it to you after school, and neither of you says anything for a full minute.

choices.label: Split the money 50-50
choices.description: Refuse to choose a winner. Allocate ₹1,00,000 to each — enough to address the worst problems in both places without fully solving either. Patch the dangerous potholes and resurface the basketball court. Replace the broken library shelves and buy 200 books. It won't be transformative, but it'll be fair. Tell both sides exactly why: because choosing one over the other would say something about this school's values that you're not willing to say.
choices.consequence_hint: Both departments get a partial fix but neither problem is fully solved — a compromise that may satisfy nobody

events.description: The library gets new shelves — sturdy, clean, properly anchored — but the book budget only stretches to 200 titles, not the 500 Mrs. Patil dreamed of. The empty spaces on the new shelves somehow look sadder than the old broken ones. The basketball court gets resurfaced beautifully, but the football field potholes are only partially filled — the worst ones, not all of them. Mr. Gupta runs his hand over the new court surface, nods, then looks at the field and sighs. Mrs. Patil arranges her 200 new books with care, then stares at the empty shelf space. Both sides come to you separately with the same sentence, almost word for word: 'It's better, but it's not enough.' Priya shrugs: 'The art of the compromise — making everyone equally dissatisfied.'

expert_pick.reason: Research shows that patience-based decisions lead to 3x better long-term outcomes.

rounds.title: The Athletes' Protest
rounds.situation:
It starts with a rumor on Monday and becomes a crisis by Wednesday. {player_name} arrives at school to find the basketball team — all twelve players, still in their sports uniforms — standing in a line outside the principal's office. Arms crossed. Faces set. Kunal Mehta is at the front, his ankle wrapped in a crepe bandage, holding a sign written on chart paper: 'OUR SAFETY MATTERS TOO.'

The story is simple and devastating: during practice yesterday, a Class 9 forward named Prashant stepped on a crack in the court, rolled his ankle, and had to be carried off. His parents are furious. They've called Ms. Sharma three times since morning. Two other parents have sent emails threatening to pull their children from the sports program entirely. The visiting coach from the district team, who was scouting players for the state selection, took one look at the court and left without watching a single game.

Kunal walks up to {player_name} in the corridor. He's not angry — he's tired, which is somehow worse. 'We didn't say anything when you chose the library,' he says. 'We understood. Books matter. But Prashant is on crutches now. The state scout left. And our inter-school match is in five days. We're not playing on that court. We're not risking anyone else's body for a school that spent two lakhs on bookshelves.'

Behind him, the team nods. Priya is standing near the water cooler, watching. She mouths one word at you: 'Careful.'

The inter-school match is Saturday. If the team doesn't play, the school forfeits. Mr. Gupta hasn't spoken to you in four days.
rounds.story: The library renovation was the right call for academics, but the athletes' pain is real and visible — a boy on crutches, a scout who walked away, parents threatening to pull their kids out. Your decision had consequences you could predict but chose to accept. Now those consequences are standing in a line outside the principal's office, and they want to know what you're going to do about it.
rounds.image_prompt: Indian school basketball team standing with arms crossed in protest, damaged sports ground visible, student leader approaching them
rounds.coaching_moment: Every decision creates a group that feels left behind. Great leaders circle back to those groups instead of ignoring them.
rounds.timer_narrative: The inter-school match is in 5 days...

choices.label: Organize emergency fundraising for sports ground
choices.description: Drop everything. Call an emergency council meeting at lunch. Launch a '5 Days to Fix the Ground' campaign — parent WhatsApp blast, teacher contribution drive, a letter to the alumni network. Put Ravi in charge of social media, Priya on parent outreach, Arjun on student donations. Tell Kunal: 'Give me five days. I'll get your court fixed before Saturday or I'll stand on it myself and apologize to every player individually.'
choices.consequence_hint: This demonstrates you care, but fundraising may not generate enough money in time

events.description: The next four days are a blur. Ravi's Instagram post about the damaged court goes semi-viral in the school parent community. Three alumni from the 2005 batch chip in ₹15,000 each. Parents contribute in amounts ranging from ₹200 to ₹10,000. The PTA president writes a cheque on Thursday evening. Final total: ₹78,000 — not enough for a full renovation, but enough to resurface the basketball court and fill the three worst potholes on the field. The contractors work through Friday night under floodlights. By Saturday morning, the court is smooth. Not perfect — but safe. Kunal runs his hand over the new surface, bounces a ball twice, and looks at you. He doesn't say thank you. He just nods. The team plays the match. They win by six points. Priya collapses into a chair after the game: 'Never again. I am never organizing a fundraiser in five days again.' She's smiling, though.

choices.label: Acknowledge their concern, hold the line
choices.description: Walk up to the team. Don't dodge, don't deflect, don't send Priya. Stand in front of twelve angry athletes and tell them the truth: the library was in worse shape, it served more students, and you stand by the decision. But also tell them this: you hear them, you see Prashant's crutches, and you personally commit to making the sports ground the number one priority for the next funding cycle. Offer to write to the alumni donor and request a second grant specifically for athletics. No promises you can't keep. Just honesty and a plan.
choices.consequence_hint: Honest and transparent, but the athletes may still boycott the match

events.description: Kunal listens with his arms still crossed, but his expression shifts — from anger to something more complicated. Frustration, maybe. But also, grudgingly, respect. 'At least you came and talked to us yourself,' he says. 'The last head boy would've sent a prefect.' The team debates among themselves for twenty minutes. In the end, they play the match — reluctantly, angrily, but they play. They lose by two points. Kunal blames the court. Mr. Gupta blames the distraction. Priya blames the universe. But something important happened: you told athletes the truth, stood your ground, and didn't lose them entirely. Your letter to the alumni donor goes out that evening. Ravi proofreads it three times. 'If this doesn't work,' he says, 'we're going to need a plan B.'

expert_pick.reason: The most effective leaders adapt their approach based on the situation — not habit.

rounds.title: The Quiet Students' Letter
rounds.situation:
It arrives on a Tuesday, slipped under the student council room door in a plain white envelope. No name on the outside. {player_name} opens it during free period and finds two pages of ruled notebook paper, covered in neat handwriting — the kind of handwriting that comes from someone who thinks carefully before putting pen to paper.

'Dear Head Boy/Girl,' it begins. 'We are the students who don't play sports. We don't win trophies or get our photos in the lobby. We spend our free periods in the library because for some of us, it's the only quiet place in the school. For some of us, it's the only place that feels safe.'

The letter goes on to describe the library in detail — the shelf near the science section that leans so badly they're afraid to pull out books, the broken chair that pinched a Class 6 boy's finger last month, the single working tube light that makes the far corner so dim that reading there gives you headaches. 'You chose the sports ground because it was loud,' the letter says. 'Athletes protest. They stand in lines. They make signs. We don't know how to do that. We just read and hope someone notices.'

Forty signatures at the bottom. Forty students who never raised their voice all year. {player_name} recognizes some of the names — the quiet girl from Class 8 who always sits in the library corner, the Class 11 boy who reads during lunch instead of going to the canteen, the Class 7 twins who share books because the library only has one copy of most novels.

Priya reads the letter over your shoulder. She doesn't say anything for a long time. Then, quietly: 'They didn't even ask for the full ₹2,00,000. They just want to know someone cares.'
rounds.story: The sports ground renovation was visible and celebrated — gleaming courts, a winning basketball team, parents posting photos. But forty students sat in a crumbling library watching the school invest in everything except the thing that mattered to them. A teacher, Mrs. Patil the librarian, told Priya last week: 'I've stopped writing grant requests. Nobody reads them.' This letter is the first time the quiet students have spoken up. It might also be the last.
rounds.image_prompt: Indian student reading a handwritten letter at a desk, run-down library bookshelves in background, thoughtful expression
rounds.coaching_moment: Leaders who only respond to the loudest voices end up serving the fewest people.
rounds.timer_narrative: The students are waiting for a response...

choices.label: Write back and create a library committee
choices.description: Write a response — not a form letter, a real one. Address it to all forty students by name. Acknowledge what you got wrong. Then do something concrete: create a Student Library Committee with five of the signatories as founding members, allocate ₹15,000 from the remaining council budget for immediate repairs, and launch a school-wide book donation drive. Pin the response letter on the library notice board where everyone can see it. Make invisibility visible.
choices.consequence_hint: This shows humility and follow-through, rebuilding trust with the quieter students

events.description: The response letter goes up on the library board on Friday. By Monday, a small crowd has gathered to read it — not just the forty signatories, but other students, even a few teachers. Mrs. Patil reads it three times. The Library Committee meets for the first time on Wednesday in the reading corner, sitting on the broken chairs they're about to replace. The book donation drive brings in 120 books in the first week — dog-eared novels, old encyclopedias, and a beautiful illustrated astronomy book donated by a Class 12 student who's leaving for college. The leaning shelf gets fixed with the council budget. Small changes, visible changes. The quiet girl from Class 8 finds {player_name} in the corridor and says, so softly you almost miss it: 'Thank you for reading our letter.' Priya watches from a distance, nodding to herself.

choices.label: Thank them but explain the safety priority
choices.description: Write back honestly. Explain that the sports ground decision was driven by safety — students were getting physically injured, and a leader's first obligation is to prevent harm. Promise that the library will be the top priority for the next budget cycle, the next donation, the next grant application. Mean it. But don't pretend the decision was wrong, because you don't believe it was.
choices.consequence_hint: Logical but feels dismissive to students who waited 8 years and will wait another year

events.description: The letter goes up on the library board. The forty students read it. Some nod — they understand the logic. But understanding isn't the same as feeling heard. The quiet girl from Class 8 reads the part about 'next budget cycle' and her shoulders drop slightly. She's been hearing 'next year' for three years. Mrs. Patil thanks you politely, but her eyes say something different. One of the letter's signatories — a Class 11 boy named Siddharth — stops coming to the library entirely. He starts spending free periods in the empty classroom instead. Priya notices before you do: 'You gave them the right answer. But sometimes the right answer isn't enough.' The library shelf finally collapses the following Tuesday. Nobody is hurt. But the symbolism isn't lost on anyone.

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: Farewell Planning — Favouritism Accusation
rounds.situation:
The Class 12 farewell is two weeks away, and the planning committee has been meeting every evening in the auditorium — seating charts, decorations, the DJ playlist, and the awards. {player_name} is reviewing the award nominations when Ravi pulls you aside near the backstage curtain, his face unusually serious.

'We have a problem,' he says. 'The Best All-Rounder award. Tara and Deepa on the committee have been lobbying for Ananya since last week. They've already told half the class she's winning. They changed the criteria twice to fit her profile — first they removed the sports requirement, then they added a 'personality' category worth 30% of the total.'

Ananya. Your friend since Class 6. The girl who sat next to you during your first exam in this school, who lent you her notes when you missed a week with dengue, who was the first person to congratulate you when you became Head Boy/Girl. She's smart, popular, and genuinely kind. But the Best All-Rounder — by any objective measure — is Karan. State-level debater. School cricket captain. 92% academics. Volunteer at the weekend teaching program. His file is twice as thick as anyone else's.

Ananya is good. Karan is extraordinary. And the committee is rigging the criteria to make sure your friend wins.

{player_name} sits in the empty auditorium after everyone leaves, staring at the two nomination files. Ananya's photo is paper-clipped to the front of hers — she's smiling, that familiar warm smile. Karan's file has no photo, just pages of achievements. Priya drops into the seat next to you: 'I know she's your friend. That's exactly why this is your call and nobody else's.'
rounds.story: The farewell is supposed to be the feel-good ending to your term — the last big event, the one everyone remembers. Instead, it's become a test of something you've been building all year: whether you actually believe in fairness or just talk about it. Ravi is uncharacteristically blunt: 'If Ananya wins and people find out the criteria were changed, everything you've done this year — the bullying case, the discipline decision, the budget fights — all of it gets a footnote: except when it was his/her friend.'
rounds.image_prompt: Indian student leader looking conflicted, two groups of students in background — one around a popular girl, another around a deserving boy
rounds.coaching_moment: The hardest ethical decisions aren't between right and wrong — they're between a friend and what's fair.
rounds.timer_narrative: The award nominations close tomorrow morning...

choices.label: Insist on transparent criteria
choices.description: Call an emergency committee meeting. Bring the original criteria — the ones from before Tara and Deepa changed them. Lay both versions on the table and ask, calmly, why the sports requirement disappeared and where the 'personality' category came from. Announce that all awards will be decided by the original, measurable criteria — academics, sports, extracurriculars, service — and that the scoring will be posted publicly on the farewell notice board. Let the numbers speak.
choices.consequence_hint: Ananya and her supporters will know you blocked them, but the process becomes genuinely fair

events.description: The committee meeting is tense. Tara goes red when you put both versions of the criteria side by side. Deepa starts to argue, then stops when she sees the other committee members nodding at your point. The scoring is published the next day. Karan wins Best All-Rounder by a clear margin. He gives a short, humble speech at the farewell that makes even the teachers clap. Ananya doesn't speak to you for two weeks. She doesn't make a scene — that's not her style — but she stops sitting next to you in class, stops replying to your messages, stops being your friend in all the small ways that friendship is built on. Priya finds you after the farewell, staring at your phone: 'You did the right thing. It just doesn't feel like it yet.' It doesn't. It really doesn't.

choices.label: Look the other way
choices.description: Close the nomination files. Tell yourself it's just a school award — a certificate and a trophy that will sit on a shelf and collect dust. It's not worth the drama, not worth the fight with the committee, not worth losing Ananya two weeks before you all leave school. Let Tara and Deepa have their way. Focus on making the rest of the farewell perfect.
choices.consequence_hint: Peace is maintained, but you'll know the process was rigged — and so will the students who told you

events.description: Ananya wins Best All-Rounder. She gives a lovely speech — she's genuinely a wonderful person, and the audience claps warmly. But in the third row, Karan sits with his hands in his lap, his face carefully neutral. His mother, who came to watch, keeps clapping long after everyone stops — she doesn't understand why her son's name wasn't called. After the ceremony, Ravi corners you: 'You know and I know and half the committee knows that was rigged. Nobody's going to say anything tonight. But they'll remember.' The student who first told you about the rigging — a quiet Class 12 boy named Ishaan — avoids eye contact with you for the rest of the evening. When you catch his glance once, the disappointment in his eyes is worse than anger.

choices.label: Talk to Ananya directly
choices.description: Find Ananya during lunch the next day. Not in front of people — in the empty chemistry lab where you both used to study during free periods in Class 10. Sit across from her and tell her everything: what you heard, what the committee did, how the criteria were changed. Don't accuse her — ask her. 'Did you know about this? Because the Ananya I know wouldn't want to win something that was handed to her.' Give your friend the chance to be the person you believe she is.
choices.consequence_hint: This preserves the friendship if she's reasonable, but she might deny it and accuse you of not trusting her

events.description: The chemistry lab is quiet except for the hum of the exhaust fan. Ananya listens without interrupting, her expression moving through surprise, confusion, hurt, and finally — something that looks like shame. 'I didn't ask them to do that,' she says. 'But I knew. Tara told me last week and I didn't stop her.' She stares at the lab bench for a long time. 'I wanted it,' she admits. 'But not like this.' The next morning, Ananya walks into the committee meeting and withdraws her name. She doesn't explain publicly — just says she wants the award to go to someone who earned it without asterisks. Karan wins. Ananya claps the loudest. After the farewell, she finds you in the corridor: 'Thank you for not letting me become someone I'd be ashamed of.' You walk home together, like old times.

expert_pick.reason: Ethical decision-making builds lasting trust — the foundation of all leadership.

rounds.title: Your Legacy Decision
rounds.situation:
The last week arrives like a held breath finally released. {player_name} sits in the student council room — the same room where Riya came crying about her tiffin box, where Neha's chemistry class stormed in demanding justice, where forty library lovers' signatures changed how you think about silence. The walls are covered in charts, to-do lists, and committee notes from a year that felt like ten.

Ms. Sharma calls you in after the morning assembly — the last assembly where you'll stand on that stage. Her office smells like jasmine and old paper. She adjusts her glasses and slides a single sheet across the desk: 'I'd like your written recommendation for the next student council president. The staff will consider it alongside their own assessments, but your opinion carries weight. You've been in the trenches. You know what this role requires.'

Two names crystallize immediately.

Meera — Class 11, universally liked, never controversial. She organized the Diwali celebration that had 100% attendance. She's warm, diplomatic, and runs the cultural committee with effortless grace. Every teacher adores her. Every student considers her a friend. She'll keep the machine running smoothly, honor your commitments, avoid conflict. Nothing will break under Meera. Nothing will change either.

Aarav — Class 11, quiet, intense, brilliant. He wrote a four-page proposal for reforming the exam feedback system that made Mrs. Deshpande raise an eyebrow in genuine interest. He volunteers at the weekend literacy program. He once told you, during a late council meeting, that he thinks the school's biggest problem isn't funding or discipline — it's that students are trained to obey rather than think. He'll face enormous resistance. But he might build something extraordinary.

The pen is in your hand. The paper is blank. Outside the window, the school grounds are bathed in golden evening light — the library with its new shelves, the sports court with its fresh paint, the assembly ground where you spoke your first words as leader. All of it, every decision and compromise and sleepless night, comes down to this: who carries it forward?
rounds.story: A hundred days ago, {player_name} stood at that microphone with shaking hands and a scribbled index card. Now the hands are steady and the card is unnecessary. You've faced bullies and budget crises, teachers who doubted you and students who believed in you, a friend's feelings and a stranger's letter, a cracked basketball court and a crumbling library shelf. Every decision left a mark — on the school, on the people in it, and on you. This is the last mark you'll leave. And it might be the one that matters most.
rounds.image_prompt: Indian student leader writing at desk with two student profiles in mind, school building in golden evening light through window
rounds.coaching_moment: The truest test of leadership is not what you build while you're in charge — it's who you choose to carry it forward.
rounds.timer_narrative: The principal needs your recommendation before the final assembly...

choices.label: Recommend Aarav — the principled choice
choices.description: Write Aarav's name on the paper. Describe his exam reform proposal, his literacy volunteering, his willingness to ask uncomfortable questions. Acknowledge that he'll face resistance — from students who prefer comfort and teachers who prefer compliance — but argue that this school has had enough smooth operators. It needs someone who believes things can be fundamentally better, not just well-managed. Hand the letter to Ms. Sharma and hope she sees what you see.
choices.consequence_hint: The school might struggle initially but will grow stronger. Your legacy is about values, not comfort.

events.description: Aarav wins the election — narrowly, by twelve votes. His victory speech is nothing like yours was. No jokes, no promises of carnivals. He talks about the anonymous complaint box and asks why it took a bullying crisis to create it. He talks about the library letter and asks why forty students had to beg for bookshelves. He talks about collective punishment and asks if fairness should depend on whether the head boy or girl happens to be brave that day. And then he says something that makes your throat tight: 'I learned what leadership looks like this year by watching someone figure it out in real time, making mistakes and fixing them. I hope to be half as honest.' Priya finds you in the corridor afterward, eyes suspiciously bright: 'Not bad for a hundred days.' Ravi just grins: 'So. What do we do now that we're not in charge?' You have no idea. It feels wonderful.

choices.label: Recommend Meera — the safe choice
choices.description: Write Meera's name. Describe her organizational brilliance, her ability to bring people together, her warmth that makes every student feel seen. Argue that after a year of hard decisions and controversies, the school needs a healer — someone who can maintain what you've built without burning out or burning bridges. Meera won't change the world. But she'll keep the world you built from falling apart.
choices.consequence_hint: The transition will be smooth but nothing will change. The problems you couldn't fix will persist.

events.description: Meera wins the election in a landslide. Her victory speech is perfect — funny, warm, inclusive. She thanks every teacher by name, promises to continue the suggestion box, and makes the whole school laugh with an impression of Mr. Gupta during sports day. The transition is seamless. She runs the council meetings on time, the events go smoothly, the cultural programs are beautiful. But by December, the anonymous complaint box has been moved to a less visible corridor. The Library Committee stops meeting. The exam feedback reform proposal that Aarav wrote gathers dust in a drawer. The school runs well. It just doesn't run forward. Ravi tells you over chai in January: 'Remember that library letter? The one with forty signatures? Meera framed it and put it on the council wall. Which is nice. But the shelf it was written about is still broken.' Priya says nothing. She doesn't need to.

choices.label: Don't recommend anyone — let students decide
choices.description: Put down the pen. Write a different kind of letter to Ms. Sharma — not a recommendation, but a proposal. Argue that the student council president should be chosen entirely by students, through a fully democratic election with open campaigning, public debates, and a secret ballot. No staff recommendations, no backroom endorsements, no thumb on the scale. Tell her that the most important thing you learned in a hundred days is that students rise when they're trusted with real responsibility. Step aside and let democracy do its messy, beautiful work.
choices.consequence_hint: This is idealistic and empowering, but removes your influence on the outcome entirely

events.description: Ms. Sharma reads your letter, removes her glasses, and looks at you for a long moment. 'In twenty-three years,' she says, 'no head boy or girl has ever given up their recommendation power voluntarily.' She approves the proposal. What follows is the most competitive, chaotic, and genuinely exciting election the school has ever seen. Four candidates. Public debates in the auditorium — real debates, with questions from the audience. Meera's campaign is slick and professional. Aarav's is earnest and detailed. A dark horse candidate, Zara from Class 11, runs on a platform of mental health support and wins the debate round. Students argue about policies in the canteen. For the first time, the election feels like it belongs to them. Aarav wins by thirty votes. His first act is to reinstate the Library Committee. Priya watches the vote count from the back of the auditorium, arms folded, smiling: 'You know what your real legacy is? It's not the complaint box or the fundraiser or the code of conduct. It's this. You taught them that their voice matters. Everything else was practice.' Ravi throws an arm around your shoulder: 'Worst head boy/girl ever. Best leader, though.'

expert_pick.reason: Ethical decision-making builds lasting trust — the foundation of all leadership.

coaching_moment: Leadership is not about having all the answers — it's about making thoughtful decisions when the answers aren't clear.

questions.question: What is 'empathy'?
questions.explanation: Empathy is the ability to understand and share the feelings of others.

questions.question: A good leader should:

choices.text: Listen to the team and consider different views

questions.explanation: Good leaders listen to diverse perspectives before making informed decisions.

questions.question: What does 'delayed gratification' mean?

choices.text: Waiting for a bigger reward instead of taking a smaller one now

questions.explanation: Delayed gratification means resisting a smaller immediate reward for a larger future one.
